title: Democracy in school
status: draft: written 18 Nov 2026 offline for Grade 4 Social Studies; not yet checked by a CBC Social Studies teacher; not loaded by the live tutor
notes: Run a real class election with a ballot box made from a carton. Name the steps as they happen.

skills.key_step: The child names democratic processes in school (secret ballot, class meetings, debates, suggestion box) and orders the election steps.

floor.prerequisite: Knows a child has rights at school.
floor.question: Name one right a child has at school.
floor.answer: any such as to learn, to be heard, to be safe

representations: step cards: nomination, campaign, voting, counting, announcing
steps: Votes are counted and the winner announced.
contexts: a class meeting on cleaning duties
a suggestion box for the school library

board.do: Write the steps in a mixed order.
Ask what happens right after voting.

misconceptions.ask: Which way of choosing a head prefect is democratic?
misconceptions.repair: Compare: who chose? how many people had a say?

misconceptions.ask: Which comes first in a school election?
misconceptions.repair: Order the steps on cards: nominate, campaign, vote, count, announce.

misconceptions.ask: How should a winner be decided?
misconceptions.repair: Hold a vote on a class song and count each hand.

listen_for: There is no reason; both are the same
misconceptions.ask: Why do we put votes in a closed box instead of raising hands?
misconceptions.repair: Ask whether a learner might vote differently if the big boy candidate is watching.

checks.question: Put in order: voting, nomination, counting, campaign.
The teacher picks the class prefect without a vote. Is this an election?

skills.key_step: The child says democracy gives everyone a voice, is fair and builds peace, and that the majority decides while others' views are respected.

floor.prerequisite: Orders the steps of a school election.
floor.question: What comes after the campaign?

representations: a story of a class that voted on a trip
steps: Say what was decided and how.
Ask how the losing side is treated.
contexts: a class voting where to go for a trip
a debate on keeping the class clean

board.do: Write: "20 learners voted for the museum, 12 for the farm."

board.say: Does the view of these 12 learners still matter?

misconceptions.ask: After a vote, what happens to the views of those who lost?
misconceptions.repair: After a class vote, ask the losers to say one idea that could still be used.

listen_for: It is not, one person is quicker
misconceptions.ask: Why is democracy good for a school?
misconceptions.repair: Compare a lunch menu chosen by one person with one chosen by the class.

misconceptions.ask: A class prefect was elected. Can she make any rule she likes?
misconceptions.repair: Ask what the prefect promised in her campaign and who she serves.

listen_for: Yes, most people voted for it
misconceptions.ask: Most of the class votes that one learner may not play in games. Is that fair?
misconceptions.repair: Ask how the left-out learner feels and what the school rules say about everyone being included.

checks.question: Give one benefit of democracy in school.
checks.answer: any of: everyone has a say, it is fair, it brings peace, decisions are accepted

checks.question: A learner lost the vote for prefect. Should the class stop listening to her ideas?
checks.answer: No: her views are still respected
